title: Study notes
html:
The idea in one minute

An X-ray image is a shadow. The tube sends a divergent (conic) beam through the patient; what the body absorbs does not reach the detector and stays white (opacity), what passes through blackens it (transparency). Everything in this chapter follows from that: why bone is white, why air is black, why a far object looks big and blurred, why contrast agents work, and why every exposure carries a small risk.

How X-rays are made and how they interact

  • Tube: heated cathode → electrons accelerated by the kV → hit the tungsten anode. 99 % becomes heat; ~1 % becomes X-rays by braking radiation (continuous spectrum) and characteristic radiation (lines).
  • kV controls penetration (energy, contrast); mAs controls the number of photons (blackening, noise) – and dose.
  • Properties to recite: electromagnetic waves at the speed of light, straight-line divergent propagation, inverse-square law, penetration, fluorescence/phosphorescence (screens, image intensifier), photographic effect (film), ionisation, biological effects.
  • Attenuation rises with atomic number, density and thickness: metal > bone/calcium/iodine/barium > soft tissue ≈ water > fat > air.

Geometry of the image – the exam favourites

  • Sharp, true-size image = object as close as possible to the detector, tube far away, small focal spot, no motion.
  • Object far from the detector → magnified and blurred (that is why the heart looks bigger on an AP than on a PA chest film).
  • Projection = the path of the beam through the body (PA, AP, lateral, oblique). Always two perpendicular views: one image is a summation of everything on the path.
  • Reading convention: you face the patient – the patient's left is on your right.

Speaking the right language

Each technique has its own words and using the wrong one is marked wrong: opacity/transparency (radiography, fluoroscopy, mammography), density hyper/hypo/iso (CT), signal hyper/hypointense (MRI), echogenicity hyper/hypo/an-echoic (US).

Contrast media – what, when, and when NOT

Iodinated (CT, IVU, angiography)Barium sulphateGadolinium (MRI)
RouteIV (oral/rectal water-soluble)Oral / rectal, digestive tract onlyIV
Main risksAllergy-like reactions, contrast nephropathy, thyrotoxicosisPeritonitis if it leaks, aspirationNSF in severe renal failure, deposition
ContraindicationseGFR < 30 or AKI (unless vital), previous severe reaction, untreated hyperthyroidismSuspected perforation, acute inflammation → use water-soluble iodineeGFR < 30 (use macrocyclic only if essential), 1st trimester

Renal rule of the course: eGFR < 30 = strongly contraindicated; 30–50 = caution with hydration; > 50 = can be given with adequate hydration. Metformin is paused around contrast in renal impairment.

Radiobiology and radioprotection

  • Deterministic effects have a threshold and severity grows with dose (skin erythema, cataract, hair loss) – seen after long interventional procedures, not after a diagnostic CT.
  • Stochastic effects have no threshold, probability grows with dose (cancer, genetic) and appear after years to decades; children are 2–3× more sensitive.
  • Three principles: justification (right test, right indication), optimisation (ALARA: lowest dose, collimation, shielding, high pitch, low mAs), limitation (dose limits for staff, not for patients).
  • Staff: time ↓, distance ↑ (inverse square), shielding (lead apron, thyroid collar), dosimeter.
  • Pregnancy: ask first; prefer US/MRI; never refuse a vital exam.

Exam reflexes

  • "White on CT" and "white on MRI T2" are different physics – calcium/blood vs water.
  • Opacity is NOT a CT word.
  • Codman, sunburst, ivory vertebra: all are X-ray (opacity) descriptions.
